lesson.title: The for Item in List Pattern: Looping Through Lists
lesson.summary: Writing for item in some_list gives you a fresh copy of each value to read, but reassigning that loop variable never changes the original list, a distinction that decides whether your loop actually edits the data.
lesson.body:
The for item in list pattern is the workhorse of list traversal in Python, and by now you have used it to read and print values. The next step is understanding precisely what item is and, just as important, what it is not. On each pass through the loop, item is assigned the next value from the list, the same way any assignment statement works. It behaves like a completely ordinary variable for the rest of that iteration.

That ordinary behavior is exactly what causes a common bug. If you try to change item inside the loop, hoping it will change the list, it will not, because reassigning a variable never reaches back into the list it came from.

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
for n in nums:
    n = n * 2
print(nums)
```

This prints:

```
[1, 2, 3, 4]
```

Even though n does double on every iteration inside the loop, nums is completely untouched. n = n * 2 just points the local variable n at a new number, it does not reach into nums and overwrite the element n came from. The list and the loop variable are connected only at the moment of assignment, after that they go their separate ways.

To actually edit a list while looping, you need a handle on each position, not just each value, so that you can assign back into the list itself using indexing. That means looping over the indices with range(len(nums)) instead of looping over the values directly:

```python
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
for i in range(len(nums)):
    nums[i] = nums[i] * 2
print(nums)
```

This prints:

```
[2, 4, 6, 8]
```

Here nums[i] = nums[i] * 2 reads the current value at position i, doubles it, and assigns the result back into that exact slot in nums, so the change sticks. The rule to internalize is simple: for value in list is perfect when you only need to read or report on data, and range(len(list)) is what you reach for when you need to write back into the list during the loop. Keep this distinction in mind, because it sets up the next tool, which gives you both the index and the value together without giving up the readability of the for value in list style.
